title: Strength in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10)
hook: a thorn in the flesh, and my grace is sufficient for thee

segments.voice: Yesterday, treasure in earthen vessels. Your line was treasure in clay. Did you notice a crack, and what it was carrying? Day five hundred seventy-eight.

Paul's critics in Corinth liked credentials: visions, revelations, impressive speech. So Paul plays their game, reluctantly. He knows a man, he says, who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven and heard words no one may speak. Most readers take the man to be Paul himself. It's the kind of story his rivals would have loved to tell. And then, just as they're leaning in, Paul stops boasting about visions and starts boasting about something else entirely: a wound he couldn't get rid of.
screen: `CRITICS WHO LIKED CREDENTIALS.` → `CAUGHT UP TO THE THIRD HEAVEN.` → `THEN PAUL BOASTS OF A WOUND.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims he calls it "a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me." The King James calls it a thorn in the flesh. The Greek word, skolops, can mean a splinter or a sharpened stake. What was it? Nobody knows, and Paul never says. Readers have guessed for centuries: an eye disease, since he mentions writing in large letters; malaria; migraines; epilepsy; a stammer; the opponents who dogged him; a temptation he couldn't shake. The silence may be a mercy. Anyone can put their own thorn in that space. What Paul does tell us is what he did. Three times he asked the Lord to take it away. And the answer was not yes. It was this: "My grace is sufficient for thee; for power is made perfect in infirmity." Paul's response turns the boasting upside down: "Gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me." The Greek for dwell is a word about pitching a tent. Christ's power camps where Paul is weakest. Then the line that sums up the whole letter: "For when I am weak, then am I powerful." Catholics have long found company here. The saints include many who lived with chronic illness, pain and limits that never lifted. The Church doesn't call suffering good in itself, and it prays for healing. But it holds that a weakness offered to God is not wasted. The thorn stayed. The grace came with it.
screen: `A STING, A THORN, A STAKE.` · `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT IT WAS.` · `THREE TIMES HE ASKED.` · `POWER MADE PERFECT IN INFIRMITY.` · then, large: `MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your thorn. Settle, and breathe. Think of one weakness you carry that hasn't gone away, however much you've wished it would. A body that hurts. A temper. Anxiety. A loss. Don't analyze it or fix it. Just name it, quietly, in one or two words. Notice how heavy it feels. If you pray, you can say Paul's answer back to God, my grace is sufficient, and stay with it. If you don't pray, simply let the thorn be named, and notice that you're still here, carrying it. The bell holds the time.
Strength in weakness. Paul's discovery when his thorn stayed: Christ's power is made perfect in infirmity. Today's word.
Your line: my grace is sufficient. Today, when your thorn shows up, say the line once, slowly, and keep going. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Many Catholics speak of "offering up" a suffering, uniting it to Christ's; the Church also prays for healing, and offers the anointing of the sick to those who are seriously ill.

original.note: Greek: a splinter or a sharpened stake. KJV 'thorn', Douay-Rheims 'sting' (2 Corinthians 12:7).

trapdoor: what you thought: a thorn in the flesh means an annoying person.
what it means: Paul's lasting weakness, unhealed after three prayers, and the grace that came instead.
what a scholar hears: skolops, a stake or splinter; its identity is unknown; 'dwell' pictures Christ's power pitching a tent over Paul.
